reviewNotes: No person has reviewed this file.

Crux is 6.2 (Cooking Oatmeal), not 6.3. IM's lesson narrative says the purpose is to introduce the two unit rates and to let students see that both describe the same situation while one may be better for a given question. 6.2 is where that happens (its narrative: “students explore two unit rates associated with the ratio”), the lesson names MP3 in Cooking Oatmeal, and IM's lesson synthesis goes back to the oatmeal table. 6.3 names the idea (“unit rate”) and practises it. 6.3 is a plausible crux too: it holds goal 3 and the term, and it would let both upstream rehearsals sit in 6.2. A reviewer may prefer that.

Because the crux is the first activity, the two upstream rehearsed moments are in the warm-up (6.1). Both rest on IM's text: responses that lack quantities, and IM's own “30 miles per hour” question. The link to the crux is that students need to hear “per” as an amount for 1 before “0.4 cups of oats per cup of water” makes sense.
Testable object: the Priya-and-Han verdict, each pair's agreed answer to “Who is correct?”. Lin's and Diego's questions and the “which rate did you use?” question test it.

IM's own moments used: the warm-up note that responses may lack quantities; IM's 30 miles per hour question (say line verbatim); the Think Pair Share and MLR3 breakdowns from the routine catalog, for routines IM lists for 6.2; the “cannot both be right” misconception in 6.2; the “not sure how to use the unit rates” misconception, the celebrated doubling strategy, and the 1/4-of-a-ticket discussion in 6.3 (say line verbatim from IM); the Three Reads breakdown for 6.3.

Premo's moments: the language moment and its by-level moves (built on IM's MLR3 support for 6.2), and the “5 × 0.4 = 2 cups of water” wrong-rate moment in 6.2. Patterns “15 ÷ 6 = 2 r 3”, the wrong-rate answer, “Priya's is the oats one” and “each rate is 1 divided by the other” are Premo's.

IM's 6.3 student response for item 4a says 28 ounces of cream cheese, which is right (0.8 × 35 = 28), but the table under it ends with the row 25 | 35; it should read 28 | 35. Nothing here repeats the 25. The transcriber also flagged it.
IM's 6.3 response 1a says “Lin’s recipe”; the task says “A cheesecake recipe”. Lin only appears in question 4a. Minor, not repeated here.

IM names the 6.2 routine “MLR3: Clarify, Critique, Correct” in the routine list and “MLR3: Clarify, Critique, and Correct” in the English-learner support. cruxLanguage.routine uses the support's spelling, as required; the routine-breakdown moment uses the list's.

produceToday is “per”, “rate” and the two rate phrases, the words students say at the crux. The unit table's only productive term for 6.3.6 is “gallon”, but it belongs to the milk problem in 6.3, not to the crux, so it is left out; “unit rate” is receptive for this lesson.

IM's 6.2 synthesis orders ideas (which rate when, then the Burj Khalifa link), not student work, so there is no which-work-first moment and no inClass.sequence. IM's narrative does say to notice pairs who use a table or a double number line; a reviewer could turn that into a share order.

Unsure: whether students at this point can divide 15 by 6 to get 2.5. IM teaches decimal division later in grade 6, so I expect table reasoning or fractions, and a “2 r 3” answer from some. That pattern is my guess, not IM's.
No optional activity in this lesson, so the cuts are shortenings only.
Student responses and the cool-down were transcribed from the Teacher Guide page images by a model, not checked by a person.

Revised 2026-10-23 after persona review: 6.3 watch-for now names the doubling-and-adding strategy (24 and 30, plus 4 and 5, gives 28 for 35) as valid, matching IM and m10; m1 reframed as a fair warm-up start, not an error (notAnError, new say, dont and criteria); m7's moves at every level now happen in the class discussion where IM places MLR3, with the same question at every level (“What does each number mean?”); added IM's oatmeal-familiarity and “oz” notes to neverCut; cruxLanguage frames all ask what each number means and why, and every level offers home language; produceToday changed from “gallon” to the crux's words; jargon (lesson synthesis, MLR3, term display, Goal 2) replaced with plain words in teacher-facing text, cruxWhy included; beforeClass trimmed to four tasks.
cruxWhy: 6.2 is where the lesson's new idea first appears: one ratio, 15 cups of water to 6 cups of oats, has two unit rates, 0.4 and 2.5, and both are right. IM's lesson narrative says the purpose is to introduce the two unit rates and to show that both describe the same situation while one may suit a question better, and the lesson's first two goals are both worked here. IM's closing class discussion for the lesson returns to the oatmeal table, and IM's language support for the activity sits in 6.2's closing discussion.

object.name: the Priya-and-Han verdict
object.what: Each pair's agreed answer to “Who is correct?”, with what each number means. Lin's and Diego's questions test it: a pair who believes both rates uses Han's 2.5 for Lin's 5 cups of oats and Priya's 0.4 for Diego's 10 cups of water.

goal: Students find both unit rates for a ratio, say what each one means in the situation, and choose the one that answers the question with a single multiplication.
rigorCheck: Does every pair still reach the Priya-and-Han verdict on their own first, say what each number means, and use both rates for Lin and Diego?

watchFor.6.1: Lists like “miles per hour” with no numbers. That is fine in a warm-up; the amounts come later.
watchFor.6.2: A pair decides only one of Priya and Han can be right.
watchFor.6.3: A pair doubles 12 and 15 to 24 and 30, then adds 4 and 5 to get 28 ounces of cream cheese for 35 of sugar. That is a valid way to share, not a mistake.

moments.see: A group's list reads “miles per hour, dollars per pound,” with no numbers.
moments.means: A fair start, not a mistake. They know “per” joins two quantities; IM expects some lists without amounts, which come later today.
moments.say: Good list. Can someone in your group give one with numbers?
moments.dont: Treat a list without numbers as wrong.
moments.evidence: Note that responses may lack quantities, such as “miles per hour” or “dollars per pound.”
criteria: Credited the list as a fair start
Invited an example with numbers without requiring it
Didn't treat the missing numbers as a mistake

moments.see: A group shares “30 miles per hour,” and the class nods and waits for the next group.
moments.means: The rate is familiar but not yet unpacked into 30 miles every 1 hour. IM uses one familiar example for that, and leaves “per 1” for later.
moments.say: What are some things we know for sure about an object moving 30 miles per hour?
moments.evidence: It is not necessary to emphasize “per 1” language at this point.
criteria: Picked one familiar rate from the class list
Asked students what they know for sure about it

moments.see: As soon as you read “Who is correct?”, partners turn and start talking.
moments.means: Without quiet think time, the first quick answer becomes the pair's verdict.
moments.say: On your own first. Two minutes, and use the table.
moments.dont: Let a quick “Han!” settle it for the pair.
moments.evidence: Students have quiet time to think about a problem and work on it individually
criteria: Protected the quiet think time before partners talk
Pointed to the table as a way in
Didn't let partner talk start early

moments.see: “They got different numbers, so one of them is wrong.”
moments.means: Different numbers look like a contradiction until each is tied to its own 1: 1 cup of water, or 1 cup of oats.
moments.say: What does Priya's 0.4 count? And Han's 2.5?
moments.evidence: Some students may think that Priya and Han cannot both be right because they came up with different numbers.
criteria: Asked what each number means in the recipe
Pointed them to where the 1 sits in each row
Left the Priya-and-Han verdict to the pair

moments.see: For Lin's 5 cups of oats, a student writes “5 × 0.4 = 2 cups of water.”
moments.means: Multiplying by a unit rate is the right kind of move; 0.4 is the rate for 1 cup of water, not for 1 cup of oats.
moments.say: In the recipe, is there more water or more oats?

moments.see: Pairs go quiet after reading “because they are not equal,” and you start rewriting it on the board.
moments.means: The flawed explanation is there for students to improve. If you fix it, they only copy.
moments.say: What would you change? Fix it with your partner first.
moments.dont: Correct the explanation for the class.
moments.evidence: for students to improve upon the written work by correcting errors and clarifying meaning.

moments.see: In the class discussion of the flawed explanation, a student points at 0.4, then at 2.5: “This one… and this one is… the other way?”
moments.means: They see the two rates are linked. The words for what each one counts aren't there yet.

emerging.say: Point to each 1. What does each number mean?
emerging.move: In the class discussion, they point to the 1 in each row and label 0.4 and 2.5 in a word, a sketch, or their home language.
emerging.nonverbal: Put a finger on the 1 in each row of the table and wait.

developing.say: What does each number mean? Tell your partner first.
developing.move: In the class discussion, they tell their partner “0.4 cups of oats per cup of water” and the same for 2.5, then help fix the explanation.

expanding.say: What does each number mean? Then fix the explanation.
expanding.move: In the class discussion, they say what each number means, rewrite the explanation with a partner to show how either rate answers the question, and make it clearer once after hearing another pair.

moments.dont: Say what the numbers mean for them.
criteria: Kept one question at every level: what each number means
Matched the way in to the student's level
Didn't say what the numbers mean for them

moments.see: On the first read of the milk situation, a student is already dividing 10 by 6.
moments.means: The first read is for what is happening. Jumping to numbers skips knowing what is asked.
moments.say: First read: what is happening here? Numbers come next.
moments.dont: Let the first read turn into solving.
moments.evidence: To ensure that students know what they are being asked to do

moments.see: A student has 0.8 and 1.25 for the cheesecake, then stops at “35 ounces of sugar.”
moments.means: They found the unit rates but don't yet see them as something to scale up, as they did with the oatmeal.
moments.say: Look at the oatmeal table. How did you get Lin's water?
moments.evidence: If students are not sure how to use the unit rates they found for each situation to answer the second half of the task, remind them of how the oatmeal problem was solved.

moments.see: A pair doubles 12 and 15 to 24 and 30, then adds 4 and 5: 28 ounces of cream cheese for 35 of sugar.
moments.means: Correct, careful reasoning that IM says to celebrate. The milk problem is where the unit rate is clearly quicker.
moments.say: That works. Would it work as fast for the milk?
moments.dont: Tell them to use the unit rate instead.
moments.evidence: Such lines of reasoning show depth of understanding and should be celebrated.

moments.see: “A quarter of a ticket per dollar? You can't buy a quarter of a ticket.”
moments.means: They are checking the number against the situation, which IM says to applaud. The rate still answers questions about money: $80 buys 20 tickets.
moments.say: If I had $80, how many tickets could I buy?
moments.dont: Agree it makes no sense and move on.
moments.evidence: Take this opportunity to applaud the student(s) for reasoning about the interpretation of the number in the context
criteria: Credited the objection as thinking about the situation
Asked them to use the rate with an amount of money
Didn't drop the rate as useless

patterns.why: They remember the words of a rate without the amounts.
patterns.evidence: Note that responses may lack quantities, such as “miles per hour” or “dollars per pound.”

patterns.why: A rate that is neither a price nor a speed, which is IM's challenge.
patterns.shows: They see “per” beyond the contexts studied so far.

patterns.says: “They can't both be right. The numbers are different.”
patterns.why: One question, one right number, from years of school maths.
patterns.shows: They checked the two claims against each other. Each number's “per 1” is the new step.
patterns.evidence: Some students may think that Priya and Han cannot both be right because they came up with different numbers.

patterns.why: Division with a remainder, not yet as 2 and 3/6 cups, which is 2.5.
patterns.shows: They know dividing water by oats gives water per cup of oats.

patterns.why: They used the rate for 1 cup of water when they knew the cups of oats.
patterns.shows: They know to scale a unit rate up by multiplying.

patterns.says: “Both. 0.4 is oats for 1 cup of water, 2.5 is water for 1 cup of oats.”
patterns.why: They tied each rate to the 1 in its row of the table.
patterns.shows: The lesson's idea: one ratio, two unit rates.
patterns.evidence: Priya and Han are both correct as shown by the table

patterns.why: Everyday words for “cups of oats per cup of water”.
patterns.shows: They know which quantity each rate counts.

patterns.says: “I used Han's for Lin because I knew the oats.”
patterns.why: They chose the rate by what the question gives them.
patterns.shows: Already choosing a unit rate and saying why, which is where the lesson is headed.
patterns.evidence: We can efficiently find how much water for 5 cups of oats using Han's rate and scaling up by 5.

predict.context: Pairs read the oatmeal recipe, 15 cups of water to 6 cups of oats. Priya says it is 0.4 cups of oats per cup of water; Han says 2.5 cups of water per cup of oats. Each student thinks alone for 2–3 minutes, then partners agree on who is correct, with a table to help.
predict.question: What will most pairs' Priya-and-Han verdict say before the class discussion?
predict.countQuestion: How many pairs will say both Priya and Han are correct before the class discussion?
predict.countUnit: pairs will say both are correct.
predict.tell: If few do, two different numbers read as one right and one wrong. That is why you ask what each number counts: the fourth moment you'll rehearse.

produceToday: cups of oats per cup of water
cups of water per cup of oats

emerging.entry: In the class discussion, with a partner, they circle 0.4 and 2.5 in the oatmeal table and mark which cup each is for, in English, a sketch or their home language, before fixing the explanation.
emerging.frame: ___ is cups of ___ per cup of ___. I know because ___.

developing.entry: In the class discussion, they tell their partner, in English or their home language, what each rate means and what is wrong with “they are not equal,” then write a better explanation together.
developing.frame: Priya's rate means ___ per ___. Han's means ___ per ___. Either works because ___.

expanding.entry: In the class discussion, they plan in English or their home language, rewrite the explanation to say how either rate answers the question, read it to another pair, and make it clearer once.
expanding.frame: The rates are not equal, but 0.4 means ___ per ___ and 2.5 means ___ per ___, so either works because ___.

cuts.note: No optional activity in this lesson. Keep the warm-up to 5 minutes: one familiar example in the share, then move on.
Skip the raffle “deal” extension, and take one student per question in the share instead of two.

neverCut: Quiet think time before partners agree in 6.2
Each pair's Priya-and-Han verdict, with a reason
The question: which rate did you use, and why?
The closing class discussion on the oatmeal table
Saying oatmeal is oats cooked in boiling water
Saying “oz” means ounces before the cheesecake problem

inClass.launch: “On your own first: who is correct? Then agree with your partner.”

beforeClass: Draw the oatmeal table on the board (water | oats: 15 | 6, then 1 | blank, then blank | 1). Fill it in as pairs share and leave it up all lesson.

Write the flawed explanation on chart paper for the class discussion at the end of 6.2: “I did not use either Priya’s rate (0.4 cups of oats per cup of water) or Han’s rate (2.5 cups of water per cup of oats) because they are not equal.”
Post three sentence frames for partner talk in 6.2: “I noticed _____ so I . . .”, “Both _____ and _____ are alike because . . .”, “How do you know . . . ?”
Start a key-words poster with “unit rate” for 6.3, and keep it up all unit.
